doc.title: Ira Gitler interviewed by Michael Woods, New York City, New York, November 16, 1995

title: Discovering Dizzy and Bird and 52nd Street in 1945-46
summary: Gitler recalls hearing Dizzy on radio from the Onyx, Groovin' High, the Spotlight Club, his first published piece, and the welcoming atmosphere of 52nd Street.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Tracing the lineage from that, from that trumpet player to another all-time favorite of mine, tell us what you know about Dizzy.

Well Dizzy I always say was one-half of my heartbeat and Charlie Parker was the other, but there are a lot of other people too, Lester Young especially and Coleman Hawkins, people like that. And many, many others. But I discovered Dizzy and Charlie Parker when I was in high school and I had already been listening to jazz for a long time, but they hit me like a revelation. I became really a fanatic about them. I tried to convert everyone I met, “You’ve got to listen to this.” And I’ve told this story a number of times but the first time I heard Dizzy, and I wasn’t aware of him in Cab Calloway’s band although I must have heard him, because my brother, among other records he collected, he loved Lunceford and Goodman and Basie especially, but he also collected Cab Calloway records. So I must have heard Dizzy without knowing it. But the first time I was aware of it was a radio broadcast on a D.J. show. There was the 1280 Club in New York on WOV, a guy named Alan Courtney, who played very good music. And one night

a week in the course of his program he would go to a live wire from some club. And this was a club on 52nd Street. In going back and doing some research, I learned it was The Onyx, and there was Dizzy and Oscar Pettiford and that, what is called the first bebop band to play, you know, as a cohesive unit, with heads that were very typical of the music as it was developing at that time. And I heard this guy playing the trumpet who was announced as Dizzy Gillespie, and I said it sounds like he’s playing some wrong notes, but he’s interesting, you know, there’s something about him that was intriguing. And I didn’t hear him again until I heard him on record. And at that time I think it was “Groovin’ High,” with Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie, and Bird hit me right away. I mean I just, you know, said what is this, it’s fantastic. And I got what Dizzy was doing also at the same time. And so you know they became like twin idols to me, and when Bird and Dizzy went to California to play at Billy Berg’s in December of 1945, I had not yet heard them in person. I wasn’t really hanging out on 52nd Street regularly until towards the end of ‘45, and they had done their famous run at the Three Deuces in May and then recorded the famous sessions for Guild, “Hot House” and “Shaw Nuff” and all that stuff. So I hadn’t heard them in person. But I was listening to all their records. And then of course the California trip was a disaster. Only the musicians were really picking up on them and the public was really not ready for them. And Dizzy came back, Bird stayed on in California. And Dizzy opened at the Spotlight Club in 1946, I think it was March, with a small band with Leo Parker on baritone in place of Charlie Parker, no relation. And I went down to hear them. And you know it just knocked me out. And the first piece of writing that I ever did on jazz that was published was in my high school newspaper, about Dizzy Gillespie at the Spotlight Club. And you know the atmosphere on 52nd Street was marvelous because once you got down there and your face became familiar, you became part of the scenery. It was almost like a stage set. It was two blocks between Fifth and Seventh Avenues. But particularly between Fifth and Sixth, that was the real concentration. But even before you were known, the musicians were very open and I remember Dizzy came by our table and I said, “When are you going to record again?” And he said, “We recorded today.” You know he had that little kind of sandpapery voice. And it turned out that was what they called the “New 52nd Street” jazz album on RCA, February 22 or something like that. And so he had recorded that day and we heard him that night. And he was an incredible personality. It was incorporated into his playing. But it was like all one, much like the other giants in the music, but some of them were more sober-sided you know, not voluble or being able to incorporate the entertainment with the high artistic quality of the music. With Dizzy you got all of that, like with Louis Armstrong. And he just was electric.
